before: Once you're in that happy place, look at the other person too, and don't go only by the one fight where they crossed your boundary, or, the other way around, by the one "no" or boundary of theirs that made you mad — after all, they're allowed to say no to you. Does it keep ending the same way, where you bring up something that hurt and then still end up reassuring them they're not a bad person, and the talk never comes back to what happened to you? (The psychologist Lindsay Gibson wrote the book on this: Disentangling from Emotionally Immature People.) Or can they hear you disagree and look at their own part?
after: You may not know for certain whether the other person is or could be capable of a healthier response, and neither do they. If they promise to change, that's probably as useful as their prior promises were. Think about how long it has taken you to become more healthy. Could you have done that from one moment to the next based on a promise? Sometimes we can be a better support for someone when we maintain a realistic boundary, so that we can hold high expectations, and still feel prepared for their failure to meet them.
brief:
- When it keeps ending the same way, it's probably not that you haven't explained yourself well enough yet.
- Go by what they keep showing they can actually do, not by what one perfect explanation might finally get through to them.
Note: the author's next paragraph ends by saying we can "hold high expectations", so this point is about what you count on, not about giving up hope. Don't word it as "lower your expectations".
Limits: don't invent facts about the author's life; say nothing more about Lindsay Gibson (she's in the paragraph before); don't say the other person is definitely the problem; don't take the next paragraph's points (you can't know for sure what they're capable of, promises, how long your own change took).
